questions.correctAnswer: The period after the Civil War when the Southern states were rebuilt and brought back into the Union
distractors: The rebuilding of Europe after World War I
The movement to rebuild Northern factories after a series of fires
The plan to build a railroad across the continent
questions.explanation: Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877. The nation had to decide how the defeated Confederate states would rejoin the Union and what rights the four million newly freed African Americans would have.

questions.question: What was Reconstruction?

questions.correctAnswer: It abolished slavery throughout the United States
distractors: It gave women the right to vote
It gave African American men the right to vote
It made all people born in the United States citizens
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery everywhere in the country, going beyond the Emancipation Proclamation, which had only freed enslaved people in rebelling states.

img.scene: A crowd of freed African American families celebrating outside a wooden courthouse in 1865, broken chain links lying in the dust, joyful historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865.
img.title: FREEDOM AT LAST

questions.question: What did the Thirteenth Amendment do?

questions.correctAnswer: Made all people born in the United States citizens and guaranteed them equal protection of the laws
distractors: Abolished slavery in the border states only
Gave the vote to all men over the age of 21
Allowed Southern states to write their own citizenship rules
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1868, the Fourteenth Amendment defined national citizenship for the first time and required states to give every person equal protection and due process - ideas courts still use in rights cases today.

img.scene: A 19th century courthouse with tall columns, a diverse crowd of citizens climbing its steps together in 1868, hopeful historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 14th Amendment: citizenship and equal protection, 1868.
img.title: EQUAL PROTECTION

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fourteen made it equal - citizenship and equal protection for all.
questions.question: The Fourteenth Amendment was especially important because it

questions.correctAnswer: The right of citizens to vote regardless of race
distractors: The right of women to vote in federal elections
The right of states to set their own voting rules without limits
The right to own land in the Western territories
questions.explanation: Ratified in 1870, the Fifteenth Amendment said the right to vote could not be denied because of race or previous enslavement. African American men voted and won office across the South - until Jim Crow laws later blocked them for decades.

img.scene: A long line of African American men in 1870s clothing waiting proudly to cast ballots at a wooden polling place, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The 15th Amendment protected Black men's voting rights, 1870.
img.title: THE RIGHT TO VOTE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fifteen let them vote - no denying the ballot by race.
questions.question: What right did the Fifteenth Amendment protect?

questions.correctAnswer: To help formerly enslaved people and poor whites with food, schools, jobs, and legal aid
distractors: To punish former Confederate generals
To sell Western land to railroad companies
To organize the return of runaway slaves to plantations
questions.explanation: The Freedmen's Bureau built schools, ran hospitals, handed out food, and helped freed people sign fair labor contracts. It founded or supported thousands of schools that educated a generation of African Americans.

img.scene: A small wooden schoolhouse in the rural South in 1867, a teacher ringing a bell as freed children carrying books hurry inside, hopeful historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Freedmen's Bureau built schools and gave aid.
img.title: SCHOOLS FOR THE FREED

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Bureau built schools and lent a hand to the newly freed.
questions.question: Why did Congress create the Freedmen's Bureau in 1865?

questions.correctAnswer: To restrict the freedom of African Americans and force them back into plantation labor
distractors: To guarantee equal rights for all citizens
To organize elections for new state governments
To set building standards for rebuilt Southern cities
questions.explanation: Black Codes limited where freed people could live and work, punished unemployment, and allowed courts to seize Black children as apprentices. Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the Fourteenth Amendment.

img.scene: A solemn scene on a Southern courthouse square in 1866, a freed family reading a posted public notice with worried faces, historical illustration with no readable words on the notice. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Black Codes restricted freed people's rights and work.
img.title: THE BLACK CODES

questions.question: What was the purpose of the Black Codes passed by Southern states in 1865 and 1866?

questions.correctAnswer: A political compromise made Rutherford B. Hayes president, and federal troops were withdrawn from the South
distractors: The Supreme Court declared Reconstruction unconstitutional
Southern states voted to end it in a national referendum
President Grant ordered all freed people to move west
questions.explanation: After the disputed election of 1876, the Compromise of 1877 gave the presidency to Hayes in exchange for removing the last federal troops protecting Black voters in the South. Southern Democrats regained control and Jim Crow followed.

img.scene: Federal soldiers in blue uniforms marching out of a Southern town at dawn in 1877, townspeople watching from porches, somber historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Compromise of 1877 withdrew federal troops.
img.title: THE TROOPS LEAVE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: In 1877 the troops went home, and Reconstruction ended.
questions.question: How did Reconstruction come to an end in 1877?

questions.correctAnswer: Allowed a Southern state to rejoin the Union once 10 percent of its voters swore loyalty to the United States
distractors: Required half of a state's voters to swear loyalty before readmission
Punished every former Confederate soldier with prison time
Gave each freed family forty acres of land
questions.explanation: Lincoln wanted to heal the nation quickly. His plan offered pardons to most Confederates and let a state form a new government once just a tenth of its voters took a loyalty oath - far gentler than Congress's later demands.

img.scene: President Abraham Lincoln seated at a desk in the White House in 1864 reviewing papers by lamplight, deep in thought, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Lincoln's plan: 10 percent loyalty to rejoin the Union.
img.title: LINCOLN'S LENIENT PLAN

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Ten percent could bring a state back - Lincoln wanted healing.

questions.correctAnswer: Sharecroppers rented land and paid with a share of the crop, often falling into debt they could never repay
distractors: Sharecroppers were required to give half their land to the government
Sharecropping families were paid high wages but charged for tools
The system gave workers ownership of the land after one season
questions.explanation: Landowners supplied land, seed, and tools on credit at high prices. When the cotton was sold, the sharecropper's share rarely covered the debt, so families had to plant again the next year - a cycle that tied them to the land almost like slavery.

img.scene: A sharecropper family hoeing a cotton field at sunset in front of a small wooden cabin, tired but together, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Sharecropping trapped families in endless debt.
img.title: THE SHARECROPPING TRAP

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sharing the crop but keeping the debt - that was the sharecropping trap.
questions.question: Why did sharecropping keep so many freed families in poverty?

questions.correctAnswer: He clashed with Congress over Reconstruction and fired a cabinet official in defiance of a law Congress had passed
distractors: He was caught taking bribes from railroad companies
He refused to free enslaved people in the border states
He tried to dissolve the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Johnson, a Southern Democrat, kept vetoing Congress's Reconstruction laws. When he removed Secretary of War Edwin Stanton despite the Tenure of Office Act, the House impeached him. The Senate acquitted him by a single vote.

img.scene: A crowded Senate chamber in 1868 during a dramatic trial, senators seated in rows listening intently, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Johnson was impeached over Reconstruction; acquitted by one vote.

questions.question: Why was President Andrew Johnson impeached in 1868?

questions.correctAnswer: 160 acres of Western land to anyone who would farm it for five years
distractors: Free railroad tickets to California
Gold mining claims in the Black Hills
City lots in the new state capitals
questions.explanation: The Homestead Act opened millions of acres of public land. A settler paid a small fee, built a home, and farmed the plot for five years to earn ownership - drawing hundreds of thousands of families west.

img.scene: A settler family building a sod house on the open Great Plains, a covered wagon and plow nearby, wide sky, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Homestead Act: 160 acres for five years of farming.
img.title: HOMESTEADERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Farm it five years and the land is yours - that was the Homestead deal.
questions.question: What did the Homestead Act of 1862 offer settlers?

questions.correctAnswer: Breaking up tribal lands into individual plots and selling the leftover land to settlers
distractors: Forbidding Native Americans from hunting buffalo
Moving all Native nations east of the Mississippi River
Outlawing the practice of Native religions in public
questions.explanation: The Dawes Act tried to force Native people to become individual farmers and give up tribal life. Native nations lost about 90 million acres - two-thirds of the land they still held - much of it sold off as surplus.

img.scene: Surveyors marking out a vast reservation into small square plots with stakes and chains, Native families watching from a distance, somber historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Dawes Act split tribal land into individual plots.
img.title: DIVIDING TRIBAL LAND

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Dawes divided tribal land - and Native nations lost most of what remained.
questions.question: The Dawes Act of 1887 harmed Native American nations mainly by

questions.correctAnswer: US soldiers killed about 300 Lakota Sioux, marking the last major armed conflict of the Indian Wars
distractors: Gold was discovered, starting a rush into the Black Hills
The Lakota defeated Custer's Seventh Cavalry
A peace treaty gave the Lakota control of South Dakota
questions.explanation: Fearing the Ghost Dance movement, soldiers tried to disarm a Lakota camp at Wounded Knee Creek. Shots rang out and the Army killed hundreds, including women and children. Historians treat it as the tragic end of armed Native resistance on the Plains.

img.scene: A quiet snow-covered valley in South Dakota in winter, tipis in the distance under a grey sky, a single eagle feather resting in the snow in the foreground, solemn historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Wounded Knee, 1890: the last major clash of the Indian Wars.

questions.question: What happened at Wounded Knee in 1890?

questions.correctAnswer: It brought hunters and settlers who slaughtered the buffalo herds the tribes depended on
distractors: It carried diseases that had never existed in North America
It forced all Plains tribes to work building the tracks
It blocked the rivers the tribes used for fishing
questions.explanation: Completed in 1869, the railroad let commercial hunters ship buffalo hides east by the carload. Within about fifteen years the herds were nearly gone, destroying the food, clothing, and shelter source at the center of Plains life.

img.scene: A steam locomotive crossing the Great Plains in 1870 while a small distant herd of buffalo grazes, dramatic sky, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Railroads brought hunters who wiped out the buffalo.
img.title: THE IRON HORSE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The iron horse arrived - and the buffalo disappeared.
questions.question: How did the transcontinental railroad hurt Plains Indian nations?

questions.correctAnswer: The main immigration station in New York Harbor, where about 12 million immigrants entered the United States
distractors: A prison for immigrants who failed medical exams
The headquarters of the New York political machine
A factory complex on the Hudson River
questions.explanation: From 1892 to 1954, immigrants arriving in New York were inspected at Ellis Island, within sight of the Statue of Liberty. Most passed through in a few hours; today about 40 percent of Americans can trace an ancestor there.

img.scene: A large brick immigration hall on an island in New York Harbor in 1900, crowds of immigrant families with bundles and suitcases walking toward it, a steamship behind, hopeful historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Ellis Island processed about 12 million immigrants.

questions.question: What was Ellis Island?

questions.correctAnswer: They crowded many families into small, dark rooms with poor sanitation and little fresh air
distractors: They were built so tall that elevators could not reach the top
They charged rents only wealthy families could afford
They were located far from any factories or jobs
questions.explanation: Tenements packed immigrant families into tiny apartments, often sharing one hallway toilet among twenty people. Reformers like Jacob Riis photographed the conditions, pushing cities toward housing codes, windows, and indoor plumbing rules.

img.scene: A crowded New York tenement street in 1900, tall narrow brick buildings with fire escapes, laundry lines overhead, families and children on the stoop, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Tenements were crowded, dark, and unsanitary.
img.title: TENEMENT LIFE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tenements squeezed whole families into one dark room.
questions.question: Why were tenement buildings a serious problem in cities like New York?

questions.correctAnswer: It made steel cheap enough to build skyscrapers, bridges, and railroads on a huge scale
distractors: It turned coal into electricity for city lights
It produced the first practical telephone lines
It made indoor plumbing affordable for tenements
questions.explanation: The Bessemer process blasted air through molten iron to remove impurities quickly, slashing the price of steel. Strong, cheap steel skeletons let buildings climb ten, twenty, then fifty stories into the sky.

img.scene: A steel mill in 1890 with glowing molten metal being poured, sparks flying, workers in protective clothing, with early skyscraper frames rising in the background, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Bessemer process made steel cheap and plentiful.
img.title: STEEL FOR SKYSCRAPERS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cheap steel built the skyscrapers - thank the Bessemer blast.
questions.question: How did the Bessemer process change American cities?

questions.correctAnswer: New workplace safety laws after 146 workers, mostly young immigrant women, died in a New York factory fire
distractors: The immediate end of the garment industry in New York
A nationwide ban on women working in factories
The creation of the first labor union in the United States
questions.explanation: Locked exit doors and broken fire escapes trapped workers when fire swept the Triangle factory in Manhattan. Public outrage pushed New York to pass dozens of safety laws - fire drills, sprinklers, unlocked doors - that became models for the nation.

img.scene: A tall New York factory building in 1911 with fire engines and long ladders below, crowds gathered in the street watching smoke rise, somber historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Triangle fire of 1911 sparked workplace safety laws.
img.title: THE TRIANGLE FIRE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Triangle fire's terrible lesson built America's safety rules.
questions.question: What did the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911 lead to?

questions.correctAnswer: To win better pay, shorter hours, and safer conditions by bargaining together
distractors: To take ownership of the factories from their employers
To keep immigrants from working in American factories
To organize workers into political parties
questions.explanation: Alone, a worker could be fired for complaining. Unions like the Knights of Labor and Samuel Gompers's American Federation of Labor used collective bargaining - and the threat of strikes - to demand the eight-hour day and safer shops.

img.scene: A hall full of factory workers in 1880s clothing raising their hands to vote at a union meeting, a speaker at the front, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Unions bargained together for pay, hours, and safety.
img.title: WORKERS ORGANIZE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Together workers bargain louder - that is the union idea.
questions.question: What was the main goal of labor unions in the late 1800s?

questions.correctAnswer: To break up monopolies and trusts that controlled whole industries and shut out competition
distractors: To protect large companies from foreign rivals
To set the prices railroads could charge farmers
To create a national bank for industrial loans
questions.explanation: Giant trusts like Standard Oil controlled nearly all of an industry and could set prices at will. The Sherman Act made monopoly conspiracies illegal, though presidents like Theodore Roosevelt later used it most forcefully as trust-busters.

img.scene: An enormous octopus-like oil trust drawn in a vintage political cartoon style looming over small factories and a capitol building, historical illustration, no readable words. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Sherman Act of 1890 targeted monopolies and trusts.
img.title: BUSTING THE TRUSTS

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Sherman went after the giants that swallowed whole industries.
questions.question: Why did Congress pass the Sherman Antitrust Act in 1890?

questions.correctAnswer: They gave jobs, food, and help to poor immigrants in exchange for their votes
distractors: They won power by promising to lower taxes on factories
They controlled the newspapers printed in foreign languages
They required voters to pass loyalty tests
questions.explanation: Bosses like William Tweed ran organizations that found newcomers jobs, coal in winter, and help with the law - then collected their votes on election day. The system genuinely helped people, but it was soaked in corruption and stolen public money.

img.scene: A portly 1870s political boss in a fancy suit handing a basket of food to an immigrant family outside a city ward office, line of people waiting, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Political machines traded favors and jobs for votes.
img.title: THE POLITICAL MACHINE

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Favors for votes - the machine's simple, corrupt bargain.
questions.question: How did political machines like New York's Tammany Hall keep power in the cities?

questions.correctAnswer: Classes, childcare, health care, and help for immigrant families in poor neighborhoods
distractors: Low-cost apartments owned by labor unions
Legal defense for political bosses accused of corruption
Training camps for new police officers
questions.explanation: Founded in Chicago in 1889, Hull House offered English classes, kindergarten, baths, clubs, and job help. Settlement workers lived in the neighborhood, learned its problems firsthand, and became leading Progressive reformers.

img.scene: A welcoming brick settlement house in 1890s Chicago, a teacher reading to immigrant children in a bright room while mothers attend a class next door, warm historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Settlement houses served immigrant neighborhoods.
img.title: HULL HOUSE

questions.question: What did settlement houses like Jane Addams's Hull House provide?

distractors: The breakup of the Standard Oil trust
Child labor being banned in every state
The United States leaving the Philippines
questions.explanation: Sinclair meant to expose the abuse of immigrant workers, but readers focused on the rotten meat. As he put it, he aimed at the public's heart and hit its stomach - Congress passed the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act in 1906.

img.scene: A muckraking writer with a notebook peering into a vast gloomy Chicago meatpacking plant in 1906, workers and hanging carcasses around him, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The Jungle led to meat inspection and pure food laws in 1906.

questions.correctAnswer: Give voters more direct power over laws and elected officials
distractors: Let the president appoint state governors
Allow businesses to veto new regulations
Shorten the terms of Supreme Court justices
questions.explanation: These reforms let citizens propose laws (initiative), vote on laws directly (referendum), and remove corrupt officials before their terms ended (recall). They were tools to break the grip of machines and special interests on government.

img.scene: Citizens in 1910s clothing signing a large petition scroll on the steps of a state capitol, eager crowd around them, historical illustration with no readable words on the scroll. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

distractors: Children were taking jobs away from union organizers
Factory owners refused to hire children over the age of ten
Children demanded higher wages than adult workers
questions.explanation: By 1900 nearly two million children worked in mills, mines, and factories, some as young as eight. Photographer Lewis Hine's images of small children beside huge machines helped push states to pass child labor and school attendance laws.

img.scene: A young boy in 1900s clothing standing beside towering textile mill machinery, looking small and tired, a reform photographer with a box camera nearby, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Child labor: long hours, low pay, no school.

questions.question: Why did Progressive reformers campaign against child labor?

distractors: Banned the sale of alcohol nationwide
Lowered the voting age to eighteen
Gave women the right to hold federal office only
questions.explanation: After decades of marches, pickets, and arrests, suffragists led by Alice Paul and Carrie Chapman Catt won the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920 - just in time for women to vote in that year's presidential election.

distractors: He lowered all railroad rates to zero
He kept the government completely out of business affairs
He sold public lands to logging companies to raise money
questions.explanation: Roosevelt's Square Deal used the Sherman Act against bad trusts, regulated railroads and food, and conserved about 230 million acres of public land. He said the government should be a referee making sure the game was fair.

img.scene: President Theodore Roosevelt in a Rough Rider style hat standing on a cliff overlooking a vast pine forest valley in the West, gesturing proudly, historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: TR: trust-busting plus conservation of public lands.

questions.question: How did Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal change the federal government?

Machines replaced all workers on the factory floor
Cars were assembled only when a customer ordered one
questions.explanation: When Ford put a moving assembly line in his Highland Park plant in 1913, the time to build a chassis fell from over twelve hours to about ninety minutes. The Model T's price dropped so much that ordinary workers could buy one.

img.scene: A 1913 Ford factory with a moving assembly line of Model T car frames, workers stationed along the line adding parts, busy historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: The assembly line made cars fast and cheap to build.

questions.question: Why did Henry Ford's moving assembly line matter so much?

distractors: Spain kept all of its colonies but paid reparations
The United States gave Cuba to Spain in exchange for trade rights
The war ended with no change in territory
questions.explanation: The Treaty of Paris (1898) freed Cuba and handed Spain's island colonies to the United States for 20 million dollars. Almost overnight, America held territory from the Caribbean to Asia.

Spain sank an American passenger ship off New York
The Spanish navy attacked San Francisco
questions.explanation: When the Maine blew up in February 1898, killing 266 sailors, sensational 'yellow journalism' newspapers cried 'Remember the Maine!' and pushed the country toward war - though the explosion's cause is still debated today.

img.scene: A American battleship at anchor in Havana Harbor at dusk in 1898, dramatic clouds overhead, Cuban shoreline in the background, tense historical illustration. No text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

distractors: China should be divided into colonies ruled by European powers
The United States should be the only nation allowed to trade with China
Chinese goods should be banned from American markets
questions.explanation: Secretary of State John Hay's Open Door notes (1899-1900) asked the great powers to keep China open to everyone's trade. The policy protected American business in Asia without the cost of ruling a colony.

The United States already had enough land for farming
European powers would declare war on the United States
questions.explanation: Members of the Anti-Imperialist League, including Mark Twain and former president Grover Cleveland, argued that a republic born by rebelling against an empire could not honestly rule other peoples without their consent.

Connect the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico
Irrigate farmland in the American Southwest
questions.explanation: The canal, finished in 1914, cut about 8,000 miles off the New York-to-San Francisco journey. Roosevelt backed Panama's independence from Colombia, then took a canal zone - a move Latin Americans long resented.

An attack on the Panama Canal by German ships
Russia leaving the war and joining Germany
questions.explanation: German U-boats were sinking ships without warning, including American vessels. The intercepted Zimmermann Telegram, offering Mexico the return of Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, outraged the public. Congress declared war in April 1917.
